source.title: Grokking of Hierarchical Structure in Vanilla Transformers
source.authors: Shikhar Murty; Pratyusha Sharma; Jacob Andreas; Christopher D. Manning

record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization on language-processing tasks using a different task and measure from the original algorithmic grokking work.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own training and generalization results and internal-property measurements. The model-depth comparisons and right-branching parsing baseline are reported results; citations to prior grokking findings are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study shows delayed ('structural') grokking in a new setting: transformer LMs on synthetic CFG-based language tasks (Dyck, Question-Formation, Tense-Inflection). It reports its own accuracy curves showing out-of-distribution generalization rising long after in-domain accuracy saturates. It is a new-setting test (T3) rather than a different method on the original question (T2).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that vanilla transformers shift gradually from memorization to hierarchical generalization with extended training ('structural grokking'). This happens most at intermediate depths. Functional tree-structuredness, unlike weight norm or attention sparsity, identifies the optimal depth. Early stopping on in-domain validation badly underestimates hierarchical generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses transformer language models trained on Dyck bracket sequences and English question-formation and tense-inflection tasks, rather than small algorithmic classification datasets. It evaluates hierarchical out-of-distribution generalization and internal tree structure.
record.method_sensitivity: Generalization varies with model depth: very shallow and very deep models often fail or exhibit the behavior infrequently, while most seeds at intermediate depth generalize.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight norms and attention sparsity grow monotonically in all models. They fail to distinguish depths that grok from those that do not; shallow models have the largest norms and sparsest attention but never generalize.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight norm and attention sparsity are not by themselves predictors of which architectures will grok.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Experiments use only three small, context-free-grammar-based datasets, and all are English-based or bracket-tracking. Results are averages across 10 seeds in the main accuracy plots, with no uncertainty estimates stated in the text. Some depth-specific values are available only in figures. The authors also state that they do not study training-data-size effects.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the tested versions were left out.

untested.parts: No small algorithmic (binary-operation) datasets are used. Dyck is a formal-language task, not the original setting. The dependence of delay on training-set size is explicitly not studied (Limitations).
No mechanistic circuit (e.g. Fourier) is identified. No removal of memorizing components is shown. There is no test that a progress measure anticipates the timing of the jump.
No realistic text, images or molecules are used (CFG-based synthetic data only). Initialization scale and weight norm are not varied, so the on/off switching and lazy-to-rich transition are untested.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Weight decay is not varied (AdamW at a fixed setting). No critical dataset size or ungrokking is tested.
Learned algorithms are not compared across runs.
The optimizer (AdamW) and numerics are not varied or controlled.

missing.what: tparseval dynamics. All models, grokking or not, induce trees close to gold syntax, matching or beating a right-branching baseline. Internal structure emerges even where generalization does not, which bears on whether gradual structure formation anticipates the jump.
missing.locator: Figure 4; Section 4.1 'Transformers are surprisingly effective at structure induction'

missing.what: Training loss flatlines around 10k steps, long before grokking. All depths reach comparable final training loss, so the depth effect is not poor optimization. This is a control establishing the delay relative to training fit.
Prior-work comparison: early-stopped accuracy below 20% versus mean about 80% with extended training, with several seeds near-perfect.

record.verdict_notes: The data are synthetic CFG-based English and bracket tasks, which is only a borderline match for V3's 'non-algorithmic data (text)'. Dyck could be argued to bear on V1, but it is not the original binary-operation setting, so V1 is left untested. Results are seed averages with no uncertainty reported. The optimizer is AdamW at lr 1e-4 with batch size 8; weight decay is not stated or varied.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not train on small algorithmic datasets such as modular arithmetic tables.

It measures tree-structuredness and other internal properties, but does not identify a Fourier algorithm, remove memorizing components, or causally show that a continuous measure anticipates the behavioral jump.

It uses small, context-free-grammar-based language tasks, not realistic text, images, or molecules; it does not vary initialization scale or test a lazy-to-rich transition or weight-norm intervention.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning is studied.
No efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking threshold is tested.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.
It does not control adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits.

rows.subject: 6-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on Question-Formation and track in-domain validation and out-of-distribution generalization accuracy.
rows.measure: Generalization accuracy; comparison of early-stopping performance with longer training
rows.baseline: <40% average generalization accuracy at early stopping based on in-domain validation
rows.value: <90% average generalization accuracy after longer training; in-domain validation accuracy had saturated before generalization improved
rows.locator: Figure 2(b); Section 3.1, 'Early stopping on in-domain validation accuracy'
rows.note: The paper reports the before-and-after values as averages across 10 seeds. It does not state that generalization begins at chance or reaches near-perfect accuracy for this average.
rows.check: The delay after in-domain saturation is clear, but mean generalization ends well below in-domain accuracy (Fig 2 gap ≈20%). The intro says the mean reaches about 80%, with only several seeds near-perfect. The paper's '<90%' wording is odd; read it as roughly 80–90%. Subject is the best depth only (6 layers), not all depths.

source_check.correct: state=observed for V3: delayed OOD improvement after in-domain validation saturation is observed. V3 does not require near-perfect final accuracy.
source_check.problem: The partial state imports a near-perfect-accuracy requirement from V1 into V3.

rows.subject: 4-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on Tense-Inflection and track in-domain validation and out-of-distribution generalization accuracy.
rows.measure: Generalization accuracy; comparison of early-stopping performance with longer training
rows.baseline: <50% average generalization accuracy at early stopping based on in-domain validation
rows.value: <80% average generalization accuracy after longer training; in-domain validation accuracy had saturated before generalization improved
rows.locator: Figure 2(c); Section 3.1, 'Early stopping on in-domain validation accuracy'
rows.note: The paper reports the before-and-after values as averages across 10 seeds. It does not state that generalization begins at chance or that the average reaches near-perfect accuracy.
rows.check: The delay is present, but mean generalization ends below 80%, short of near-perfect. Subject is the best depth only (4 layers).

source_check.correct: state=observed for V3: delayed OOD improvement after in-domain validation saturation is observed. Initialization and weight-norm interventions remain untested.
source_check.problem: Final mean accuracy below 80% does not make the observed delay partial under V3.

rows.subject: 6-layer transformer
rows.operation_detail: Train on Dyck and track in-domain validation and generalization accuracy.
rows.measure: Generalization accuracy over training, alongside in-domain validation accuracy
rows.note: The text says generalization improves many steps after in-domain accuracy saturates across datasets, but gives no Dyck-specific numerical value in the text.
rows.check: Dyck-specific values are figure-only and the extracted gap labels (∆≈0%, 2%, 8%) are garbled. Only the general 'across datasets' sentence covers it, so the magnitude cannot be read.

rows.subject: Transformers with 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 layers
rows.size_stated: 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 layers; hidden dimensionality 512; 4 attention heads
rows.operation_detail: Compare model depths by the fraction of random seeds whose generalization accuracy eventually crosses 80%.

conditions.value: very shallow and very deep versus intermediate depth

rows.measure: Fraction of seeds eventually exceeding 80% generalization accuracy
rows.value: Text reports that very shallow and very deep models are unsuccessful or do so infrequently, while most seeds generalize at intermediate depth; exact fractions are figure only
rows.note: The text describes the depth pattern but does not give the per-depth fractions.
rows.check: Delayed generalization occurs mostly at intermediate depth. Very shallow and very deep models fail or rarely cross 80%. Per-depth fractions are figure-only.

rows.subject: Transformers across model depths

conditions.value: All model settings; data-dependent measurements use 10k training examples

rows.value: The score improves over time for all models; the optimal-depth model learns the most tree-structured solution compared with shallow and deep models
rows.locator: Figure 3(b); Section 4.1, 'Optimal models are most tree-structured'
rows.note: The result is an association over training and depth; the study does not establish causal formation of a generalizing circuit or show that the metric anticipates the behavioral change.
rows.check: Tree-structuredness rises gradually in all models, including ones that never generalize. It is highest for the optimal depth but is only said to 'coincide' with grokking; the paper does not show it anticipates the jump in time. It is a cross-depth discriminator, not a temporal progress measure, and no memorization-removal phase is shown.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V2. Tree-structuredness increases across models and is greatest at the optimal depth; circuit formation, subsequent removal of memorizing components, and anticipation of a behavioral jump are not established.
source_check.problem: The structural proxy cannot establish V2's circuit-development and anticipation mechanism.

rows.subject: Transformers across model depths
rows.operation_detail: Measure normalized parameter weight norms during training and compare their ability to distinguish grokking model depths.

conditions.value: Weight norms normalized by number of layers

rows.measure: Normalized weight norm and whether it differentiates model depths that generalize
rows.value: Weight norms grow for all model settings but do not differentiate good from bad architectures
rows.locator: Figure 3(b); Section 4.1, 'Optimal models are most tree-structured'
rows.note: The paper explicitly says weight norms do not predict which depths generalize.
rows.check: Weight norm is observed rather than intervened on, and is used only to discriminate depths. It does not measure V2's circuit formation or V3/V5's weight-norm switching. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Transformers across model depths
rows.operation_detail: Measure attention sparsity, using negative mean entropy of attention distributions, during training.
rows.measure: Attention sparsity and whether it differentiates model depths that generalize
rows.value: Attention sparsity increases for all model settings but does not differentiate good from bad architectures
rows.locator: Figure 3(b); Section 4.1, 'Optimal models are most tree-structured'
rows.note: The paper explicitly says attention sparsity does not predict which depths generalize.
rows.check: Attention sparsity is not a measure any version names. Move to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Best-depth transformers on Question-Formation (6L) and Tense-Inflection (4L), synthetic CFG language data
relationships.reason: OOD generalization rises far after in-domain validation saturates: <40%→~80–90% and <50%→~80% means (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Mean out-of-distribution accuracy rose from below 40% to roughly 80–90% on Question-Formation and below 50% to roughly 80% on Tense-Inflection, long after in-domain saturation.

source_check.condition: Best-depth transformers on Question-Formation (6L) and Tense-Inflection (4L), synthetic CFG language data
source_check.reason: R1 and R2 directly show delayed OOD improvement after in-domain validation saturation. Initialization and weight-norm switching are untested.

relationships.condition: Depth sweep 2–10 layers on Question-Formation and Tense-Inflection
relationships.reason: Delayed generalization depends on architecture: very shallow and very deep models rarely or never grok (R4). Even at best depth, mean generalization stays below near-perfect (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Very shallow and very deep models rarely or never grokked, and even the best depths achieved imperfect mean generalization.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Depth sweep 2–10 layers on Question-Formation and Tense-Inflection
source_check.reason: R4 establishes architectural dependence: shallow and deep models fail or grok infrequently compared with intermediate depths. Below-near-perfect endpoint accuracy is not independently a limitation of V3.

relationships.condition: Tree-structuredness (tscore) dynamics across depths, Question-Formation and Tense-Inflection
relationships.reason: A continuous internal structure measure grows gradually and is highest at the grokking depth. It also grows in non-grokking models and is only shown to coincide with, not anticipate, the jump (R5).
relationships.display_finding: The internal structure measure grew gradually and peaked at the grokking depth, but also increased in models without grokking and coincided with rather than preceded the jump.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Tree-structuredness (tscore) dynamics across depths, Question-Formation and Tense-Inflection
source_check.reason: R5 measures a structural proxy and its association with successful generalization. It does not identify a generalizing circuit, track removal of memorizing components, or test anticipation of the jump. These untested components cannot justify limits_scope; growth in unsuccessful models alone does not contradict V2.

relation.reason: Its own training curves and depth comparisons test the occurrence and architectural dependence of delayed generalization.

tranche.reason: The study reports delayed hierarchical generalization in a new setting: transformer language models trained on CFG-generated language tasks.

source_check.notes: All datasets are CFG-generated; this is not evidence from realistic large-model training. Section 3.1 gives endpoint bounds, not exact final means; per-depth success fractions are figure-only.

statements.correction: Tree-structuredness increases in all models; optimal-depth models have the highest tree-structuredness; shallow models never generalize hierarchically; temporal anticipation and removal of memorizing components untested.
statements.problem: The observation about this study is correct, but its use as a V2 limits_scope result overstates what was tested. Increasing tree-structuredness in unsuccessful models does not establish failure of V2's anticipatory mechanism.
